Article Title: What an ideal PG should look like: A checklist
Article Text:
Despite housing significantly more occupants, many such PGs do not require a fire NOC or adhere to the safety standards applicable to commercial premises.

WHAT A PG SHOULD HAVE: A CHECKLIST

Structural safety:

Emergency lighting:

Fire extinguishers on every floor:

Broad staircases:

Emergency exits:

Digital records of inmates:

Access for emergency vehicles:

Adequate ventilation and windows:

Smoke detectors and alarms:

Safe electrical systems:

Fire-fighting equipment:

Safe kitchen and cooking area:

No overcrowding:

Emergency preparedness:

First-aid & emergency contacts:

WHAT MASTER PLAN DELHI 2047 SAYS ABOUT PGs

HOW REGULATORY GAPS QUEER THE PITCH

Buildings less than 15 metres height do not require NOC from fire department.

PGs do not require registration or permission.

No official figure on how many of them are operational in Delhi.

Most of them have basements and structural alterations.

Norms related to their location based on road-width as per MPD 2021 are often flouted.

Residential units converted into PGs, leading to overcrowding.

No audit of such establishments.

— An IIT-Delhi professor

— PROF VK PAUL | DIRECTOR, SCHOOL OF PLANNING AND ARCHITECTURE, DELHI

— ATUL GARG | FORMER FIRE CHIEF





Residential units are increasingly being converted into commercial hubs under the tag of paying guest accommodation, often without the safety infrastructure expected of a commercial establishment.A typical residential flat may house a family of four or five people, whereas a PG can accommodate 12-15, with three or four occupants often staying in a single room. This significantly increases the occupancy load on the building.Despite housing significantly more occupants, many such PGs do not require a fire NOC or adhere to the safety standards applicable to commercial premises.Building plan should be sanctioned. The design of building should meet safety norms, including seismic safety standards.Backup lighting and illuminated exit signs to guide occupants during a power failure or fire.Easily accessible, regularly inspected, with training given to occupants on how to use them.Staircases should be accessible, unobstructed and designed to easily accommodate total number of occupants in a building.Exit routes should be clearly marked and kept free of obstructions.Digital records of occupants and staff should be maintained.It should have proper road-width to give access to emergency vehicles like fire tenders.Rooms should have sufficient ventilation.Detectors should be installed in rooms, corridors and common areas, with a functional alarm system.No loose wiring, overloaded sockets, makeshift connections or exposed electrical equipment.Hose reels, hydrants and other required firefighting equipment should be installed and maintained regularly. Deployment of security guards, police verification of staff.Cooking facilities should be properly ventilated, with safe LPG and electrical connections.The number of occupants should be appropriate for the size and design of the rooms and building.Occupants should know what to do in case of an emergency like fire or earthquake. Emergency numbers should be displayed prominently.A first-aid kit and prominently displayed emergency numbers should be availableHostels and PG accommodation will not be permitted in A & B colonies (A & B colonies are graded residential areas based on their market value and infrastructure quality).“Such buildings need repair and retrofitting on a regular basis. Besides, any modification to the structure of the building should be checked and approved.”“PG accommodations are essentially private hostels and should provide basic assurance of building structure safety, fire and life-safety standards, including adequate exits, CCTV cameras for security in common areas, women-safe premises, showers for emergency vehicles and clearly displayed dos and don’ts on use of alcohol and narcotic substances. There must be compliance with the basic framework or a simple policy for PGs under the Ease of Doing Business framework, mandating a clear set of safety and operational rules for owners. ”“ If a PG is housed in a building less than 15m in height, it is not required to obtain a fire safety NOC. Whenever a residential unit is converted into a high-occupancy or commercial activity, it needs to be assessed whether the building has adequate structural stability, staircases and exits to safely accommodate the increased number of people. Another major gap is regulation, as PG accommodation currently do not have a licensing or registration mechanism. ”
Article Summary: A typical residential flat may house a family of four or five people, whereas a PG can accommodate 12-15, with three or four often staying in a single room. Despite housing significantly more occupants, many such PGs do not require a fire NOC or adhere to the safety standards.

Article Title: DU’s hostel crunch is more than a decade-old problem. Can Delhi learn from universities abroad?
Article Text:
Miranda House, for example, has an overall student strength of 5,375, but its hostel accomodates only about 370 students.

71 DU colleges without hostels





NEW DELHI: For thousands of students coming to Delhi University from outside the city, securing admission does not necessarily mean securing a place to stay.Only a handful of colleges have hostels and admission into them is harder than getting into university to begin with.The gap has fuelled a thriving private PG economy around college clusters. The shortage is not new. In a written reply to a Rajya Sabha question in Nov 2016, Union human resource development ministry, citing DU, said the university had 19 hostels with a combined capacity of 3,580 students.Including accommodation provided by some colleges, estimates put hostel availability at 6,000 seats, while DU admitted at least 60,000 students annually.A decade later, the gap remains substantial. In 2026, DU has 91 colleges, with 69 colleges and departments participating in undergraduate admissions. Around 71,600 new UG students were admitted in 2026-27, while about half of DU students are from outside Delhi, as per college estimates. Against this, there are around 7,000 hostel seats. The university has 20 main hostels across its North and South campuses, while 20 colleges have hostel facilities and 71 do not, according to officials.The numbers become starker against DU’s overall student population. Its 2024-25 annual report, the latest available on its website, records 2.1 lakh undergraduate students and 34,520 postgraduate students, including PhD scholars -- nearly 2.5 lakh in all.Miranda House, for example, has an overall student strength of 5,375, but its hostel accomodates only about 370 students. For 2026-27, the college has offered just 90 hostel seats to first-year students. Sri Venkateswara College, with an overall student strength of around 4,600, has hostel capacity for 150 students, with just 50 seats available to first-year students.Residence has, in fact, figured in DU’s governing framework since its early years. Section 33 of Delhi University Act, 1922, says every student, other than one studying through correspondence, “shall reside in a college or a hall, or under such conditions as may be prescribed by the ordinances”. A university official, however, said the provision “in today’s times should not be read as a guarantee of a university hostel room to every student”.For students arriving from another state, an admission confirmation can therefore mark the beginning of another search for somewhere to live. Limited hostel seats leave many turning to PGs, private hostels and rented flats in areas such as Vijay Nagar and Malka Ganj, near North Campus, and Satya Niketan, near South Campus.Students say the private market can mean paying more for cramped and poorly maintained accommodation. “There should be more hostels for students. Outside, everything is expensive and not maintained. I don’t know where students are supposed to go,” a DU student said.Reliance on private housing is not unique to Delhi. What differs in some university systems abroad is the support provided to students navigating the private rental market.Indroneil B Biswas, who studied in Oregon in the US, recalled that a department administrator contacted him even before his arrival about applying for campus accommodation with another international student. “The admins helped us navigate on-campus housing,” he said, though accommodation was not automatic. Universities there also provide off-campus housing listings, information on tenants’ rights and, in some cases, access to student legal services for housing disputes.In Manchester in the UK, Manchester Student Homes, a university-run service, helps students navigate private accommodation through listings and an accreditation scheme requiring participating landlords and agents to follow a Code of Standards. It also offers housing advice and assistance with disputes. In Australia, universities, including University of Melbourne, similarly provide off-campus housing platforms and guidance on the private rental market, including students’ rights and responsibilities as tenants.
Article Summary: 71 DU colleges without hostels and admission into them is harder than getting into university. The gap has fuelled a thriving private PG economy around college clusters. Miranda House, for example, has an overall student strength of 5,375, but its hostel accomodates only about 370 students.

Article Title: Maharashtra unwraps gifts for Maratha youths on 10th day of Manoj Jarange fast
Article Text:
In photo: Manoj Jarange





CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: With Manoj Jarange’s indefinite hunger strike for Maratha reservation entering its 10th day, Maharashtra govt on Monday announced a series of concessions for Maratha, Kunbi and SEBC youths, even as the quota activist intensified his attack on Mahayuti and called on supporters to gather at Antarvali Sarati on Sept 12.State issued four govt resolutions (GRs) covering education, scholarships, hostel assistance and skill development, apparently seeking to defuse mounting anger within the Maratha community.The decisions include extending educational concessions available to OBC students to Maratha students from the 2026-27 academic year, releasing Rs 200 crore towards pending hostel maintenance allowances, revising SARTHI’s overseas scholarship policy and providing free driving and conductor training to 1,440 Maratha and Kunbi youths.The developments came amid growing concern over Jarange’s health. The activist, who has intermittently accepted saline support during the protest, has reportedly stopped consuming water and is refusing medical treatment.Despite the announcements, Jarange blamed chief minister Devendra Fadnavis and deputy CM Eknath Shinde for delaying reservation benefits for the community and appealed to Marathas to assemble at Antarvali Sarati on Sept 12 to decide the next course of the agitation, including a possible march to Mumbai.Under one of the GRs, all educational benefits currently available to OBC students will be extended to Maratha students through the Directorate of Technical Education and universities from the next academic year.The higher and technical education department has also released Rs 200 crore for pending Dr Punjabrao Deshmukh hostel maintenance allowances for EBC, EWS and SEBC students. The funds have been made available through supplementary demands approved during the monsoon session.In another significant decision, govt revised the SARTHI overseas scholarship scheme. Tuition fees will now be paid directly to foreign universities; the earlier funding ceiling has been removed. Students will also receive an additional annual maintenance/contingency allowance of $1,500, or £1,100. A new merit-listing mechanism based on QS rankings has also been introduced. A fresh merit-listing system based on QS rankings has also been introduced.SARTHI has additionally tied up with the Institute of Driving Training and Research, Pimpri-Chinchwad, to provide free LMV, HMV and conductor training to 1,440 Maratha and Kunbi youths from Oct 1, with a target of ensuring employment or self-employment for at least 1,000 beneficiaries.Meanwhile, revenue minister Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil reviewed the process of displaying Kunbi records traced from historical documents, including the Hyderabad Gazetteer, at the village level. In Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, the records have been uploaded on the district administration’s website and can be accessed through mobile phones. Gram panchayats have also been instructed to display records pertaining to their respective villages.
Article Summary: State issued four govt resolutions (GRs) covering education, scholarships, hostel assistance and skill development. The decisions include extending educational concessions available to OBC students to Maratha students from the 2026-27 academic year. The developments came amid growing concern over Manoj Jarange’s health.

Article Title: Schools facing acute teacher shortage in core subjects: TISS
Article Text:
(AI image used) Across ten states, schools are struggling with significant teacher shortages in vital areas such as math and science

Resources stretched thin





MUMBAI: Schools surveyed across 10 states - Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Telangana, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Punjab, Odisha and Mizoram - report acute teacher shortages in fundamental subjects such as mathematics and science (35%), English (31%), and in regional languages (30%). Moreover, it was found that only 51% of mathematics teachers studied the subject at under-graduate level, highlighting credential mismatches.Govt schools face recruitment delays and staff shortages (33% reported staffing challenges), but little retention difficulty. Private schools, on the other hand, recruit faster but face higher teacher attrition (as reported by 14%), especially in rural areas (18%).These are some of the findings from the executive summary of the biennial report on the 'State of Teachers, Teaching and Teacher Education for India' (SoTTTER) 2025 by TISS Centre of Excellence in Teacher Education (CETE) released on Teachers' Day. The SoTTTER 2025 focuses on three landmark policies that reached key implementation milestones in 2025 - 15 years of the Right To Education Act (2009), 10 years of the Rights of People with Disabilities Act (2016), and five years of the National Education Policy (2020).Comparing the data from the SoTTTER 2023, the report highlighted a critical aspect of the student enrollment falling sharply by 1.55 crore in five years - from 26.5 crores in 2021-22 to 23.2 crores in 2024-25. At the same time, the teaching workforce grew by six lakh, thereby improving the average student-teacher ratio. The report also highlighted 'an accelerated privatisation and feminisation of the teaching force'. Women now make up 54% of the teaching workforce, up from 51% in the previous report. However, a clear urban-rural gap remains - women comprise 67% of urban teachers, while rural schools remain male-dominated, with women accounting for only 47%.The summary of SoTTTER 2025 also underscores a worrying rise in multi-grade classrooms in govt schools, where a single teacher instructs students from multiple grades. In 2025, nearly half of govt primary schools operated as multi-grade classrooms, up from 38% recorded in 2023.The report, which reviewed the structural and pedagogical shifts in the Indian teaching workforce, will be officially released in Oct this year, in collaboration with the Language and Learning Foundation.Prof Padma M Sarangapani, former chairperson of CETE, currently Dean of IMSE, Mahindra University, and principal investigator of the study, noted that while many aspiring teachers are genuinely motivated to enter the profession, the lack of job security and employment opportunities acts as a disincentive. Nearly half of the teachers surveyed also felt that the profession is misunderstood and that their work is not sufficiently valued or appreciated. "Another major concern is the delayed recruitment process, which can sometimes take seven to eight years. With no guarantee of securing a job, this uncertainty can significantly demotivate young aspirants," she said. The report also gives recommendations for resolving the persistent teacher shortages.Apart from the national datasets from the U-DISE+ 2024-25 and Periodic Labour Force Survey 2024-25, the report used primary data from the field survey covering 499 schools in the 10 states. Some of the positive developments include improved working conditions for teachers, reduction in single-teacher schools, and increase in the numbers of teachers with greater local connect.
Article Summary: Across ten states, schools are struggling with significant teacher shortages in vital areas such as math and science. Only 51% of mathematics teachers studied the subject at under-graduate level. Government schools face recruitment delays and staff shortages, but little retention difficulty. Private schools, on the other hand, recruit faster but face higher teacher attrition.

Article Title: Bank staff not ‘public servant’ under IPC: Bombay HC
Article Text:
Bombay HC

Set aside assault charge





NAGPUR: An employee of State Bank of India (SBI) cannot be treated as a “public servant” under IPC’s Section 21 merely because he’s a bank employee, the Nagpur bench of Bombay High Court has held, quashing a criminal charge against a 65-year-old educationist, who was accused of assaulting a public servant.Justice Mehroz Pathan, last week, allowed the criminal revision by Madhukar Pawar, resident of Akola district. The judge set aside the district sessions court’s Nov 2025 order, which rejected Pawar’s discharge application and framed a charge against him under Section 353 IPC.The case arose from a complaint by an SBI employee. Pawar’s counsel, V R Deshpande, argued that Section 353, which criminalises assault against a public servant to deter him from performing official duty, could not be invoked because the complainant himself did not fall within Section 21’s definition of a public servant.Justice Pathan accepted the argument, relying on earlier rulings of Delhi and Bombay high courts concerning the status of bank employees under IPC. He also examined Supreme Court’s 2016 judgment in CBI, Bank Securities & Fraud Cell versus Ramesh Gelli, which the prosecution cited to contend that bank employees were public servants.The State, represented by additional public prosecutor Prachi Joshi, relied on Supreme Court’s interpretation of Section 46-A of Banking Regulation Act, 1949.“The apex court’s observations in the case of Ramesh Gelli show the accused, who was a bank employee, was not a public servant within the meaning of Section 21 of IPC,” Justice Pathan observed.The court said the same principle had to apply to the bank employee who was the complainant in the present case.“For proving the offence under IPC’s Section 353,” the court said, three essential clauses need to be established: the victim must be a public servant; the accused must have committed an assault or used intentional criminal force; and the act must have been intended to prevent or deter the public servant from performing official duties.“In so far as other offences under Sections 504 and 506 of IPC are concerned, the same are non-cognisable offences,” the judge further held. Since the Section 353 charge itself was not sustainable and the requisite magistrate’s permission under Section 155 of Code of Criminal Procedure had not been obtained, those offences too could not stand in the case, it said.The court consequently quashed the Nov 1, 2025, order rejecting Pawar’s discharge application and set aside the order framing the Section 353 IPC charge against him.
Article Summary: Madhukar Pawar, 65, was accused of assaulting a public servant. The case arose from a complaint by an SBI employee. The judge set aside the district sessions court’s Nov 2025 order, which rejected Pawar's discharge application and framed a charge against him.

Article Title: CBI court acquits Acharya Balkrishna in passport forgery case
Article Text:
In photo: Acharya Balkrishna





DEHRADUN: A CBI court has acquitted Patanjali Ayurved co-founder Acharya Balkrishna and co-accused Naresh Chand Dwivedi in a long-standing case concerning allegations that Balkrishna fraudulently obtained an Indian passport using forged educational certificates.The case, investigated by CBI’s Anti-Corruption Branch in Dehradun, originated from a 2011 representation alleging that Balkrishna was a citizen of Nepal rather than India and had dishonestly secured an Indian passport.The prosecution’s case centred on documents submitted in 1998 to the regional passport office in Bareilly, where Balkrishna was accused of using two certificates purportedly issued by Sampurnanand Sanskrit University in Varanasi: a Purva Madhyama certificate submitted as proof of date of birth and a Shastri certificate submitted to obtain emigration check not required status.CBI alleged that the roll numbers on the certificates belonged to other individuals—identified during the probe as Kamal Singh and Leela Prasad Bhattarai—rather than Balkrishna, and that Naresh Chand Dwivedi, then principal of Sri Radha Krishna Sanskrit Mahavidyalaya in Khurja, had made handwritten entries on the contested documents.Consequently, Balkrishna faced charges under Section 471 of the IPC and Section 12(1)(b) of the Passports Act, 1967, while Dwivedi was charged under Section 466 of the IPC in a prosecution led by Ram Kumar for CBI, Dehradun.According to the defence counsel, the court’s decision to acquit hinged on several key weaknesses in the prosecution’s case, including the failure to prove forgery or track down the identity and whereabouts of the actual students whose roll numbers appeared in the university registers. The other factors include the disputed admissibility of secondary evidence under the Evidence Act and flaws in the handwriting analysis where expert opinions relied on photocopies rather than original documents, creating reasonable doubt regarding whether the questioned writing could be attributed to Dwivedi.The defence also successfully raised doubts regarding the allegations by pointing out that Balkrishna later passed the Acharya examination from the same university after completing the Purva Madhyama and Shastri courses.
Article Summary: A CBI court has acquitted Patanjali Ayurved co-founder Acharya Balkrishna and co-accused Naresh Chand Dwivedi in a long-standing case. The case stemmed from allegations that Balkrishne fraudulently obtained an Indian passport using forged educational certificates.

Article Title: Satya Niketan building collapse: DU students seek hostels, safety steps, accountability
Article Text:
Students said the Satya Niketan tragedy exposed enforcement failures, with illegal construction, alleged collusion and safety violations putting lives at risk.





NEW DELHI: The Satya Niketan building collapse, just a few steps from Delhi University’s South Campus, has left students worried about where they should stay and how.Monday, students marched from the arts faculty to the VC’s office, holding up banners that said, “200 acres of land is lying vacant, yet no hostel for students.” Another read, “Provide accommodation to students. It is our right.”Students’ organisations such as Disha, All India Democratic Students Organisation (AIDSO), Students Federation of India (SFI) and Krantanikari Yuva Sangathan (KYS) also participated in the march. Anger over the lack of affordable and safe accommodation is what brought the students out to the protest.For Himantri, the tragedy hit close to home. Her hostel is next to the building that collapsed. “It is frightening to see something like this happen next door. It is not as if students do not pay rent. Many of us are paying as much as Rs 20,000 for a room, yet our lives remain at risk. Even my building is very old. This is not just about what happened to these students. We need to ensure no one else suffers the same fate,” she said.Tarunima, who lives with her family in Delhi, said she joined the march out of concern for her friends who live in paying guest acommodations or PGs.“My friend lives in a PG and it is pathetic... It feels so wrong that so many students have no safe option,” she said.Chiranshu, another protester, said students were demanding immediate compensation for the victims and a serious rethink of the university’s hostel policy. “This is not the first such incident. Hostels are available to only around 3.5% of students. Most of them are meant for boys, while some hostels are also closed. Where are the rest of the students supposed to go?” he said.Students alleged that the Satya Niketan tragedy reflected a larger failure of enforcement, with illegal construction, alleged collusion among landlords, builders and authorities, and violations of safety norms putting lives at risk. For them, however, the problem begins much earlier. Why are DU students being pushed into expensive PGs and flats in the first place?They said areas such as Kamla Nagar, Vijay Nagar and Satya Niketan have become hubs for students looking for accommodation, often leaving students dependent on ageing or poorly maintained buildings.They demanded that DU immediately reopen hostels that have remained closed for years and use its available land to build more accommodation. They also called for affordable student housing and regular safety audits of buildings in student-dominated areas.The Satya Niketan collapse has triggered protests beyond the campus. ABVP held a late-night protest Sunday and entered the MCD office, demanding the commissioner’s resignation.On Monday, ABVP held protests and sit-ins across several Delhi University colleges, demanding accountability and stronger student safety measures. Demonstrations were held at Hansraj College, Hindu College, Kirori Mal College, Ramjas College, Shaheed Bhagat Singh College and several other campuses. The ABVP demanded a high-level probe into the building collapse, strict action against negligent PG operators, building owners and officials, and immediate structural and safety audits.ABVP national general secretary Dr Virendra Singh Solanki said: “No student in Delhi should ever risk his life by living in an unsafe building.”
Article Summary: Satya Niketan building collapse has left students worried about where they should stay. Anger over the lack of affordable and safe accommodation is what brought the students out to the protest. Demonstrations were held at Hansraj College, Hindu College, Kirori Mal College, Ramjas College, Shaheed Bhagat Singh College.

Article Title: BMC demolishes garage, marriage hall over encroachment on fire station land
Article Text:
The K-West ward of the BMC has initiated the demolition of illegal structures on Chitrakoot Grounds, freeing up crucial space reserved for a fire station





MUMBAI: BMC’s K-West ward on Monday demolished an unauthorised garage and marriage hall operating from Chitrakoot Grounds on Link Road, Andheri. The action followed complaints that the premises had encroached on open space reserved for a fire station.Local BJP corporator Rupesh Sawarkar said he had been pursuing the issue since his election earlier this year. He said he found that the encroachments had also extended onto a portion of the land reserved for the proposed fire station and had been urging the civic authorities to act.Monday’s demolition, Sawarkar said, takes the locality “one step closer” to getting a full-fledged fire station. The area currently lacks one, a concern given the high-density residential belt along Lokhandwala and Link Road.Sawarkar said he is now pursuing the authorities to expedite the process of developing the fire station so that construction can begin at the earliest. “The land is being freely used for wedding functions, film shoots and turf cricket activities through lease arrangements, leading to financial irregularities,” said Sawarkar.Dhaval Shah from the Lokhandwala Oshiwara Citizens Association said that there has been a reservation in the BMC’s Development Plan for a fire station since 1991.“The BMC should continue the momentum and make it a reality as lakhs of Versova Assembly residents need it. With massive skyscrapers in the making, fire safety must be a top priority,” he said, adding that the absence of a nearby fire station has affected emergency response times in the area, resulting in delays during fire incidents and increasing the risk of loss of life and property.
Article Summary: BMC’s K-West ward on Monday demolished an unauthorised garage and marriage hall operating from Chitrakoot Grounds. The action followed complaints that the premises had encroached on open space reserved for a fire station. Local BJP corporator Rupesh Sawarkar said he had been pursuing the issue since his election earlier this year.

Article Title: As Samsung turns 30 in India, JB Park lauds country's role as Global Innovation Hub for the company
Article Text:
JB Park, Samsung South West Asia President and CEO

India has evolved from being a market where global technologies were introduced to a country helping imagine, engineer and develop technology for the world, Samsung South West Asia President and CEO JB Park said as Samsung marks 30 years in India. “What inspires me most about India is that it constantly exceeds expectations,” Park said. “Today, we don’t look at India just as a market of 1.4 billion people. We see India as a place where the future of technology is being imagined, developed and led.”Samsung entered India in 1995. Over the past three decades, as India transformed into one of the world’s fastest-growing digital and innovation economies, Samsung expanded its manufacturing footprint, strengthened its research and design capabilities and invested in building an innovation ecosystem in the country.“The story of Samsung in India has never been about selling products. It has been about growing together,” Park said. “But more importantly, we evolved from bringing technology to India to creating technology with India.”“India challenges us to innovate differently,” Park said. “Building products for a country of this scale and diversity means designing solutions that are intuitive, inclusive and relevant to millions of people with very different needs.Those innovations often go on to benefit consumers around the world.”As artificial intelligence transforms consumer technology, Samsung’s engineers in India are also collaborating with global teams to develop next-generation AI experiences.“AI will only be meaningful if it solves real problems for real people. And, there are few places that challenge us to do that better than India,” Park said. Samsung’s investments in India have also extended beyond manufacturing and R&D to talent, skills, education and innovation.“Technology does not create progress on its own. People do,” Park said. “We believe human potential is the most important technology platform of all.”As Samsung marks three decades in the country, he said the company's legacy in India should ultimately be measured not only by the products, manufacturing ecosystem and research capabilities it has helped build, but by the people and ideas it has helped nurture.“I don’t believe our legacy will ultimately be defined by the devices we made,” Park said. “I believe it will be defined by the dreams we helped unlock.” “If Samsung can play even a small role in helping shape that generation, it would be our greatest achievement in India,” he added. “Because the most enduring technologies are not always the ones we build. Sometimes, they are the ideas we ignite in people.”
Article Summary: Samsung entered India in 1995. Over the past three decades, as India transformed into one of the world’s fastest-growing digital and innovation economies, Samsung expanded its manufacturing footprint. “The story of Samsung in India has never been about selling products. It has been about growing together,” Samsung South West Asia President and CEO JB Park said.

Article Title: SAP has a message for all software companies, after stock goes down by over 20%: Pendulum will swing back, as ...
Article Text:
SAP has a message for all software companies

SAP stock rebounds after SaaS sell-off

SAP says AI will not easily replace mission-critical software

SAP sees another challenge emerging: the rising cost of using AI

SAP is changing how it charges for AI

SAP is telling the software industry not to write off traditional SaaS companies as AI changes how businesses build and buy software. Despite SAP's stock falling by more than 20% over the past year amid the wider “SaaSpocalypse”, SAP global president of customer success and Americas Jan Gilg believes the sell-off has gone too far. “As usual, I feel the pendulum will swing back,” Gilg told Business Insider. Gilg further added that there will be “users,” “losers and winners” and said he believes SAP will be among the winners.The comments come as AI tools from companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI raise questions about whether businesses will continue paying for traditional software. SAP, Salesforce and Workday have all faced pressure as investors assess how AI could change the software market.SAP's shares have recovered strongly after the company reported its latest earnings in late July. The stock has risen roughly 40% since the results, helped by cloud growth and progress in business AI.Gilg described the earlier sell-off as “a bit of an overreaction on the entire industry.” He said SAP is responding by investing in AI and data while also changing how it charges customers.“Everybody has AI on the agenda right now,” Gilg said.One concern during the SaaSpocalypse has been the rise of “vibe coding”, where AI tools can help people create software without traditional programming methods. Gilg said SAP does not currently see customers replacing its software this way, particularly when it comes to critical business systems.“It's really multifaceted. On the one side, there was the idea that customers will vibe code their software themselves rather than buying packaged software. We don't see that frankly,” Gilg said. “We don't see that, especially for mission-critical purposes. It's not just about features and functions. It's about auditability, governance, and the maintenance of the software.”He said SAP's role could become more important as companies look for ways to connect AI with business data and existing systems.Gilg said companies are already seeing higher “token costs”, referring to the amount of AI usage they pay for. He expects businesses to look more closely at whether their AI spending produces measurable results.“Customers are seeing token costs go through the roof already,” Gilg said. “How do you measure and control that, and how do you show an outcome for that? Budgets won't necessarily increase. It will still have to come from somewhere. Therefore, the scrutiny will become much, much bigger.”“We do see new players out there from Anthropic, OpenAI, Palantir, and so on,” Gilg said. “That's going to be the battlefield of the future.”SAP is also changing parts of its pricing strategy as AI becomes a bigger part of its products. The company is moving some services from traditional subscription models toward consumption-based pricing, where customers pay according to how much they use.“What outcome are they driving?” Gilg said. “That's how we charge the consumption of those agents, which is very transparent to customers. Also, it's much easier to justify why they would actually pay for it. That's the current model many are following.”
Article Summary: SAP CEO Jan Gilg believes the sell-off of SaaS companies has gone too far. He said there will be “users,” “losers and winners” and SAP will be among the winners. SAP is responding by investing in AI and data while also changing how it charges customers.

Article Title: Duolingo launches ‘learn English from Punjabi’ course
Article Text:
Duolingo partners with Airtel to offer 12-month super subscription

Duolingo, the world’s leading mobile learning platform, has announced the launch of its new “Learn English from Punjabi” literacy course, aimed at making English learning more accessible to Punjabi speakers in India and across the globe. The course went live on September 7, 2026, and is now available on the Duolingo app.Spoken by more than 100 million people worldwide, Punjabi is one of the most widely spoken languages, with vibrant communities in India, Canada, the UK, the US, and Australia. Written in Gurumukhi script, Punjabi carries a rich literary and cultural heritage. The new course allows learners to begin their English journey directly from Gurumukhi, helping them build skills for education, careers, and global connections.This marks Duolingo’s second regional language course for North India after Hindi, and adds to its growing portfolio of regional offerings, which already includes Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, and Tamil.Karandeep Singh Kapany, Regional Marketing Director for India and South East Asia, said: “Being able to launch this course in my mother tongue is incredibly meaningful and a moment of real pride for me. Punjabis have long embraced opportunities beyond borders.By making English learning available in Punjabi, we’re helping remove language barriers and enabling more people to access the opportunities that English can unlock. ”In another news, recently Duolingo partnered with Airtel to provide 12 months of Super Duolingo at no additional cost to Airtel’s 376 million subscribers.The partnership will give Airtel customers access to Duolingo’s premium ad-free learning experience, including unlimited energy, AI-powered real-time speaking practice, personalised exercises, and mistakes review. The subscription will be available across mobile, Wi-Fi, and DTH services, accessible through the Airtel Thanks App, with no credit card required.Language skills are increasingly becoming gateways to education, careers, and global opportunities. Airtel’s collaboration with Duolingo extends its focus on differentiated customer experiences by offering millions of users an engaging way to build language skills and develop consistent learning habits.
Article Summary: Punjabi is one of the most widely spoken languages. Written in Gurumukhi script, Punjabi carries a rich literary and cultural heritage. This marks Duolingo’s second regional language course for North India after Hindi.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences

In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.
